title: Coding finite sequences: pairing and bounded decoding

based_on.title: Computability and Incompleteness
based_on.pages: 28–30 (§2.4, finite sequences, bounds, and simultaneous/history recursion; version 2007-01-09)

based_on.title: Formalizing Computability Theory via Partial Recursive Functions
based_on.venue: 10th International Conference on Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP 2019)
based_on.pages: 12:2–12:7 (§§2–3.1, square pairing and primitive-recursive data operations)

summary: Encode finite lists as natural numbers, prove explicit decoding bounds, and derive primitive-recursive list operations and recursion on finite histories.
abstract: A single natural number can record an entire finite list, including its length and any zero entries. To use such a code in a calculation, we need more than the knowledge that finite lists are countable: we need concrete ways to read and change the encoded data. We begin by arranging pairs of numbers in successive square shells, then use those pairs to attach one entry to a coded list. Decoding always moves to a smaller number, which gives an explicit bound on every traversal. Length, indexed access, reversal, and concatenation can therefore be computed by primitive recursion. The same construction explains how an ordinary recursion can keep several values together, or retain all its earlier values for the next step.
